scrollVideo.name: Frames played by scroll
scrollVideo.summary: A 90-frame image sequence drawn on a canvas; the scroll position decides which frame is shown. There is no video tag.
scrollVideo.note: Scroll progress is converted to a frame number and the canvas draws that image. Scrolling back draws the frames in reverse the same way, with no stutter.
scrollVideo.captionOneBody: Scroll progress becomes a frame number; the canvas only paints that frame.
scrollVideo.captionTwoBody: There is no playback timeline; scrolling back draws the frames in reverse order.
scrollVideo.failed: The frames didn't load — reload to try again

dissolve.name: Noise dissolve transition
dissolve.summary: An image removed step by step with a noise field and a threshold, so the edge of the dissolve is irregular.
dissolve.note: The field is the sum of three parts: a vertical gradient sets the overall direction, low-frequency fbm makes the edge irregular, and high-frequency speckle adds detail. The threshold sweeps across the screen as you scroll.
dissolve.headline: An irregular dissolve edge
dissolve.body: The position of the edge is computed from the noise field and the threshold, so it advances at a different rate in each place.
dissolve.tail: Scroll back and the image is restored the same way.
dissolve.fallback: No WebGL available here, so this falls back to the static composition.
dissolve.saveData: Data Saver is on, so the shader was never loaded; this is the static composition instead.

meltingText.name: Text melting into place
meltingText.summary: The text is first blurred so the letters stick together, then becomes sharp letter by letter.
meltingText.note: A gaussian blur spreads the edge of each glyph, and an alpha threshold turns everything above 30% opacity solid. Where two blurred neighbours overlap, they join.
meltingText.label: Melt · once, on entering

grove.name: A procedurally grown mossy root
grove.summary: A moss-covered root generated entirely in code, with no model files: swept tubes, a moss cushion, ferns, flower sprays and two hundred and thirty thousand instanced blades of grass.
grove.note: All progress in the scene is computed from the scroll position: where the survey front is, how bright the wireframe is, how long the moss is, when the flowers open and where the butterfly is. The pointer is the only live input: the view tilts with it, the moss parts under it, pollen rises where it passes, and the perched butterfly flaps its wings when the pointer comes close. This part runs only while something is still changing; once the pollen has settled, the tilt has returned and the butterfly is still, rendering stops. Study 21 uses the same moss (the same lib/grove). It used to be the home page's cover; since September 2026 it is only in the lab.
grove.headline: Generated from one seed
grove.body: One random seed decides everything: the path of the root, which side the moss grows on, where the ferns are and where each blade stands. After a reload the result is identical.
grove.tail: Move the pointer through the moss. Scroll back and the growth reverses.
grove.fallback: No WebGL available here, so this falls back to the static composition.
grove.saveData: Data Saver is on, so the scene was never loaded; this is the static composition instead.
grove.specPassesValue: Two bark plates baked the moment there is a renderer, once per page; a single scene render per frame after that.
grove.specAssetsValue: No textures and no model files; it loads only its code.
grove.specGeometryValue: All generated from one seed: swept tubes, a moss cushion that is thicker on the lit side, ferns, flower sprays, and {blades, number} instanced blades ({bladesSmall, number} on a narrow viewport).
grove.specVariantsValue: {count}, switchable at the top right. The geometry is the same; the materials, fog and sky colour differ.
grove.specPixelRatioValue: The display's own, capped at 2 — and at 1.5 once the canvas passes 2.6 million pixels.
grove.specFallbackValue: With no WebGL, or for a reader on save-data, this is a static composition instead.

liquidMetal.name: Liquid-metal button
liquidMetal.tagline: A WebGL2 dispersion shader in five passes
liquidMetal.summary: The metal look of the button is computed in a shader, with no gradients or textures. A scalar field goes through a smoothstep, and each wavelength is sampled at a slightly different height, which produces the rainbow edge.
liquidMetal.note: The scroll shows the render pipeline in three stages: the first has only the dispersion field, with sharp edges; the second adds the blur and the moving rim; the third adds bloom and the contrast curve, which gives the final metal. The button works the whole time: it responds to hover, press and keyboard focus. The animation runs only while you interact with it or while it is still settling. The main button on the home page's first screen is this one.
liquidMetal.headline: The rainbow edge is computed
liquidMetal.body: The width of the rainbow edge equals the dispersion divided by the magnitude of the field's gradient. So the same shader gives very thin rainbow lines where the field changes quickly, and broad navy-to-cyan transitions where it changes slowly.
liquidMetal.tail: Press and hold the button, then let go: a crease runs along the rim.
liquidMetal.fallback: No WebGL2 available here, so this falls back to the button alone.
liquidMetal.label: Hold it down

workstation.name: A 3D desk you can drag to spin
workstation.summary: A 3D desk model from the old portfolio: it turns to face the front on entry, the screens slowly change brightness, and after a drag it keeps turning with inertia.
workstation.note: The original model was 8.5 MB; gltf-transform (Draco + 1024px WebP) brought it down to 1.1 MB, and the Draco decoder is self-hosted. It loads only when it enters the viewport, renders at 30 fps while idle and at full rate during a drag, and is not loaded at all under Save-Data. The wheel controls zoom only in the area directly over the desk; elsewhere the page scrolls as usual. The two arrows at the lower right turn it an eighth of a circle per press, for keyboards and touch screens.

workstation.deskAria: A 3D model of a gaming PC desk

lensSlider.name: Lens-distortion slideshow
lensSlider.tagline: Three.js shader + a lens for a transition
lensSlider.summary: A slideshow of four photographs. On a change, a circular lens grows from the centre of the frame with the next picture inside it; the distortion is strongest near the rim and disappears once the circle covers the frame.
lensSlider.note: The shader takes two pictures and one progress value. The circle's radius grows with the progress, and every pixel inside is shifted toward the centre by its closeness to the rim raised to the fifth power, so only a narrow band next to the rim is magnified and the middle is not distorted. Once the radius passes half the diagonal the circle covers the frame, and the rest of the progress removes the magnification. The rim also has a ring of water ripples that weakens with the progress; the original site has it and TTTISE's breakdown does not. Each step of the scroll switches the lens to the next picture; scroll back partway through and the lens shrinks again. Based on Oscar Pico's project slider (oscarpico.es), implemented from TTTISE's breakdown of it.
lensSlider.fallback: No WebGL available here, so this falls back to a plain change of picture.
lensSlider.saveData: Data Saver is on, so the lens was never loaded; this falls back to a plain change of picture.
lensSlider.riverAlt: A river valley in fog, one person standing on a rock midstream
lensSlider.riverBody: A river valley in fog, with one person standing on a rock in the middle of the river.
lensSlider.fallsAlt: A waterfall dropping into a green valley in a forest after rain
lensSlider.fallsBody: A forest after rain, with a waterfall dropping into the valley.
lensSlider.seaAlt: The sea from above, with white foam
lensSlider.seaBody: The surface of the sea and its foam, photographed from above.

lensSlider.coffeeBody: By a window in the morning, hot water poured in circles over the grounds.

neon.name: The La La Land neon sign
neon.tagline: SVG lettering traced from the film's sign + a filter for the tube + a GSAP flicker sequence
neon.summary: A blue neon sign on a brick wall, with Mia & Sebastian's Theme and a few stills. The sign is traced from the one over the door of Seb's in La La Land, with the name changed to mine.
neon.note: The sign uses no font. The lettering comes from a vector traced from the film's sign and published on Wikimedia Commons (Seb's.svg, Espandero, CC BY-SA 4.0): the ring's centre and radius, the angles of its two gaps, the ends of the bar, and the outlines of the S and the note are measured directly from it. The original has no F or H. The F is the original E without its bottom arm; the end of its stem has the same rounded shape as the arms, and the short piece of the middle arm that extends left past the stem is kept. The H is two stems joined by a bar as heavy as the E's middle arm, with edges at the same slant. The letters are upright and the baseline rises 9.5° to the right. The ring leaves a gap at the top right for the note's stem; its left arc ends at the lower left, and its right arc continues round the bottom into the bar, as one continuous tube. The letters are drawn as solid shapes and the tube is produced by a filter: feMorphology erodes the shape inward by 13 units, and subtracting that from the original leaves a band of constant width along the outline, which is also how a real neon sign follows the edge of the lettering. The white core is eroded from that band, the glow is the band dilated and blurred, and the four layers are merged. The brick wall is painted once on a canvas: each brick gets a random hue and lightness, a highlight along the top, a shadow along the bottom and a layer of grain; it is not repainted after that. Lighting up follows a fixed flicker sequence: the ring flickers a few times, then the bar, then the letters one at a time. The sign is also the switch: turning the light off stops the music, and turning it on lights the sign again and resumes the music. The same sign is used at the site's entrance: it is shown first when the home page is opened directly, and the entrance transition goes through the ring (see the study on the entrance transition through the sign). The music is the site's background music. The player is in the layout and the audio file is self-hosted (Hurwitz's Mia & Sebastian's Theme, 3 minutes 19 seconds, looped), with no third-party player embedded. Playback is attempted once the sign is fully lit; if the browser blocks it, it is tried again on your first click on the page. After that, the note button on the top navigation controls it. Below are the stills from /films/lala, in the order of the story.
neon.galleryLede: Stills from La La Land, in the order of the story.
neon.credit: Sign lettering after Seb's.svg by Espandero on Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0); used here as a personal homage only.

sideways.name: Text that scrolls sideways
sideways.summary: As you scroll down, the sentence moves left. The section is pinned for one screen, the vertical scroll distance is converted one to one into horizontal movement, and each character returns to its place from a random height and angle as it crosses the screen.
sideways.note: The pin distance equals the width by which the track overflows, so the text moves one pixel for each pixel scrolled (the ease has to be none). Each character has its own ScrollTrigger whose containerAnimation points at the horizontal tween, so "left 100% → left 40%" is measured in horizontal progress. The horizontal layout (a full-height stage, a max-content track, a 100vw lead-in) is written by GSAP as inline styles inside a matchMedia branch; the server output and touch devices get an ordinary centred paragraph that only fades in. The text is split again after a locale switch. The slogan on the About page uses the same component (fx/SidewaysBand).
sideways.lead: Up to here the page scrolls vertically.
sideways.lineOne: This line moves left as you scroll.
sideways.lineTwo: 这行字随滚动向左移动。
sideways.tail: From here the page scrolls vertically again. Scroll back and the characters scatter the way they came.

masthead.name: Home headline, rising line by line
masthead.summary: The entrance of the home page headline: each line rises from below its own mask.
masthead.note: Each line is wrapped in overflow hidden, and the inner element rises from 112% to 0 over 1.05s on expo.out, with 110ms between lines. On the home page it is a CSS transition triggered by the opening animation; here it is a GSAP tween triggered on entering the viewport, so it can be replayed. "Again" remounts the two lines, which is what happens on a route change.
masthead.label: Home headline · line mask
masthead.lineTwo: as it was when we first met

reveal.name: Scroll entrance: fade and rise
reveal.tagline: The site's one scroll entrance · power2.out 0.6s
reveal.summary: How lists and content blocks enter across the site: they fade in while moving up from 24px below, each child 60ms after the previous one. It is the site's only scroll entrance.
reveal.note: The Reveal component: y 24, opacity 0 → 1, 0.6s on power2.out, triggered once at "top 85%"; with a stagger, the children are 60ms apart. The content is always in the DOM (server-rendered and indexable). GSAP hides it on the client just before the tween starts, and only by opacity, never visibility: transparent content stays in the tab order and in find-in-page, so when keyboard focus reaches it the browser scrolls to it and the entrance plays. Only the first twelve children are staggered; the rest enter together with the twelfth, so the end of a long list does not wait. When the tween ends, clearProps removes transform, opacity and visibility, leaving no inline styles, so hover tweens and Flip elsewhere read clean elements. "Again" remounts the list.
reveal.label: List · y:24, staggered
reveal.itemOne: The first row enters from 24px below
reveal.itemFive: No inline styles are left afterwards

headline.name: English post titles, decoded letter by letter
headline.summary: The entrance of an English post title: each position shows a few random lowercase letters before stopping on the right one.
headline.note: PostTitle chooses the entrance by whether the title contains Chinese characters. An English title gets one 0.9s ScrambleText pass with a lowercase-only character set, speed 0.6 and revealDelay 0.15, so each position changes through a few lowercase letters before it stops. A Chinese title does not use this, because swapping in a character of a different width on every frame only looks like noise; its entrance is the study on Chinese post titles. "Again" remounts the title, which is what happens on a route change.
headline.label: Headline · decode
headline.title: On side projects, and why they stay small

unmask.name: Chinese post titles, rising line by line
unmask.summary: The entrance of a Chinese post title: each line rises from below its own mask, and the lines are split again once the font has loaded.
unmask.note: PostTitle uses this when the title contains Chinese characters: SplitText splits it into lines, masks each line and runs yPercent 110 → 0, 80ms apart. It looks similar to the home headline study; the difference is how the lines are made. The home page's two lines are fixed in the markup, while these are split by SplitText at runtime from the actual width. autoSplit is required: when this code runs for a Chinese title the font files have usually not finished loading, and lines split against the fallback font break in different places once Yozai loads. autoSplit splits again after the font loads and rebuilds the tween from its current progress. "Again" remounts the title.
unmask.label: Headline · line mask
unmask.title: 一封写给数字修士的信

magnetic.name: Magnetic buttons
magnetic.summary: The button shifts toward the cursor and its label moves a little further than its plate; when the cursor leaves the range, both layers spring back. Three buttons show three strengths, and the dotted ring marks the range.
magnetic.note: Based on GSAP's demo azmKBBJ: the box is measured once on pointerenter (once per hover, not per frame), pointermove multiplies the cursor's offset from the centre by a strength and writes it as x/y, and the inner layer moves 0.6x further; on leave both layers spring back on elastic.out. The first version attached the listeners to the layer that moves, which caused two problems. At ×0.75 the plate and the inner layer together moved 1.2x the cursor's offset, faster than the cursor, so the cursor was always over the button, pointerleave never fired, and a button could be dragged across half the screen. Near the boundary it also switched repeatedly between leave and enter, which showed as jitter. Now there are three layers: the outermost never moves and only listens and is measured, with a 20px hit area around it; the plate and the inner layer move separately. Whether the cursor is still in range is decided from the resting box plus the hit area, regardless of where the plate currently is. Mouse-type pointers only.
magnetic.label: Magnet · three strengths
magnetic.reachNote: The dotted ring is the range: the pull starts when the cursor enters it and stops when the cursor leaves, regardless of where the button currently is.
magnetic.touchNote: There is no magnetic effect on touch screens; it works with a mouse only.

glint.name: A rim light that follows the pointer
glint.tagline: feSpecularLighting · the light follows the pointer
glint.summary: A highlight on the card's rim that follows the pointer; only the edge lights up. The top navigation uses the same effect.
glint.note: This is how the top navigation does it: a 1.5px white ring whose filter uses feSpecularLighting with SourceAlpha as the surface and an fePointLight as the light, then feComposite in clips the highlight back to the ring's own alpha, so only the edge is lit. The light's x and y are in the ring's own filter coordinates, which is the cursor position minus the card's top-left corner; each pointermove eases them over 0.3s on power2.out so the light moves smoothly. On the navigation the light stays above the capsule's top edge and follows x only. The card here is wider, so the light follows both x and y, sits higher (z 36) and has a broader hotspot (exponent 12), and the whole rim shows a highlight as the pointer crosses. Mouse-type pointers only.
glint.label: Rim · highlight follows the pointer
glint.cardBody: Move the pointer across the card. The part of the edge nearest the pointer lights up.
glint.touchNote: There is no such effect on touch screens; it works with a mouse only.

dieCut.name: The die-cut sticker outline
dieCut.summary: The white outline of the site's stickers: the element's alpha is grown outward and filled white. One filter, three radii.
dieCut.note: The outline is feMorphology dilate: SourceAlpha is grown by N pixels and filled white, and the original is drawn back on top. It needs no JavaScript and renders on the server; the three thicknesses are the same filter with different radii. The tilt uses the standalone CSS rotate property and not transform, because the sticker wall's Draggable writes transform, and this way a dragged sticker keeps its tilt. Only content uses the sticker style on this site, and the number of stickers is limited.
dieCut.label: Edge · three radii

stickerWall.name: A sticker wall you can throw
stickerWall.summary: The sticker wall on the About page: stickers fly in from an arc above to their positions, wiggle on hover, and can be dragged and thrown with a mouse.
stickerWall.note: The entrance uses polar coordinates: each sticker starts on an arc above the wall and lands in its position on elastic.out(1, 0.5), 50ms apart. Hover is a CustomWiggle on rotation only, so it does not conflict with the transform the drag writes. Dragging is Draggable + Inertia: edgeResistance adds resistance when a sticker is dragged past the edge, and minimumMovement 10 keeps a click from counting as a drag. On release, one or two small stickers from a pool of eight fly out and fade upward. Dragging is enabled for mouse-type pointers only: on a phone, capturing swipes over an area this wide would stop the page from scrolling, so on touch screens the stickers are a static row. The words on the stickers are technical terms that are the same in both languages, so they have no translated copy.
stickerWall.label: Sticker wall · draggable
stickerWall.wallHint: Throw with a mouse · tap on a phone

peel.name: A sticker that peels back on click
peel.summary: The sticker over the email address in the footer: a corner lifts on hover, and a click folds it up along its top edge, shows its back and fades it out. React toggles a single boolean.
peel.note: A pure CSS state machine: React toggles one boolean and everything else is a transition on transform and opacity. The fold is rotateX with perspective 520, and the grey back is visible partway through. The lift is done by cross-fading the opacity of two shadow layers; box-shadow itself is not animated, because it repaints on every frame. Clicking again (or using the keyboard) sticks it back. While the sticker is in place, the link under it has tabIndex -1 and aria-hidden, so Tab does not reach it. The large sticker in the corner of the 404 page can be peeled off completely (the crease is a clip-path). Here the sticker covers a sentence; in the footer it covers the email address.
peel.label: Peel · one boolean

scatter.name: Particle text the pointer scatters
scatter.summary: The line of text on the 404 page: it is sampled into particles, the pointer pushes them apart, and they return on springs when it moves away. Once all of them are back, the animation loop stops.
scatter.note: The sampling uses the paragraph's own computed font and box, so the text does not move when the canvas takes over. Each dot is a discrete spring: v ← f·(v + e·(target − pos)). The determinant of the state matrix is always f, and when underdamped the displacement envelope decays by √f per frame, so the settling time depends on f alone (1.1s to reach 1%) and the ease only affects the overshoot. Each dot's ease is slightly randomised so the dots do not move in step. The pointer pushes away dots within 90px, and still has an effect a short distance outside the canvas. Once every dot is back, requestAnimationFrame stops; pointer movement, a resize or a theme change starts it again. Mouse only: on touch screens it is ordinary text.
scatter.label: Scatter · gather
scatter.touchNote: There is no such effect on touch screens; it is shown as ordinary text.

dotName.name: A name hidden in dot noise
dotName.tagline: 7×7 dot fields · superellipse rim · shallow sphere
dotName.summary: The name on the About page: each letter is a grid of dots surrounded by noise, and every dot's brightness changes slowly. When the pointer is over it, the noise dims and the letters appear.
dotName.note: Each letter is a 7×7 dot glyph placed in a field one cell larger on every side, and that extra ring is all noise. The field's edge is cut with a superellipse of exponent 4: a circle would cut off the corners of F and H, a square would look like the stickers' die-cut edge, and exponent 4 is in between. The cutoff radius is also slightly randomised, so the edge is uneven. The grid is projected onto a shallow sphere, so the spacing is wider in the middle and tighter at the edge; this shape does not change on hover. Every dot is a small ellipse at a random angle whose brightness changes independently. When the pointer is over the field, the noise dots dim and the dots on the strokes brighten. The glyph table covers A–Z only. Mouse only: on touch screens it is a static field.
dotName.label: A name in the noise
dotName.touchNote: There is no such effect on touch screens; it is shown as a static field.

approach.name: A window that opens onto the moss
approach.tagline: CSS sticky + clip-path window + WebGL2 dissolve
approach.summary: Formerly the second and third sections of the home page, now only here. As you scroll, a window opens in the page and shows the moss rendered live behind it; of the two paper cards, one is below the canvas and one above it. After a hold, the next page covers it again with a dissolve.
approach.lede: Scroll down about three screens: a window opens in the page and shows the moss growing, it holds for a while, and then the next page's paper colour covers it again. Move the pointer inside the window: the two paper cards shift by different amounts.
approach.note: What is pinned here is a window, so it uses CSS sticky and not ScrollTrigger's pin: a pin-spacer needs the page height to be measured while Lenis is smoothing it, and sticky needs no measuring. ScrollTrigger only provides progress. The section is 320svh tall: the first 42% is the entrance (the rounded clip-path window opens on outQuad and the scene scales from 1.16 to 1), then a hold, and from 62% the paper colour comes down from the top. Its edge uses the same threshold field as the noise dissolve study, except that here it draws the paper colour. There are two paper cards in the window. Card a has no z-index, so it is painted below the canvas and the trunk passes over the empty area at its lower right; card b has z-index 3 and is in front of the root. This ordering is only possible with a scene rendered live; a static picture cannot do it. The two cards are the same size and sit at 860 × 160 and 1237 × 482 on the stage's 1600 × 880 grid. In the pointer parallax they shift by different amounts, which shows the distance between them. Between the opening and the cover, the whole screen is moss; during that time body gets data-grove-immersed, and the header's paper-colour scrim is hidden.
approach.title: The moss through a window
approach.linkLabel: See the study where the moss is generated

segmented.name: The sliding highlight on filter tabs
segmented.summary: The highlight that marks the selected option in the software page's filter: on a change it slides from the previous option to the new one.
segmented.note: The indicator is a single element. On a change, Flip.getState records its position, it is moved to the new slot, and Flip.from plays the difference between the two positions, so it slides over from the previous slot. The first placement is not animated, because there is no previous state. When the window width changes its position is measured again without animation. The arrow keys also move between options. The reshuffling of the tiles in the grid is a separate study.
segmented.label: Segmented control · sliding highlight
segmented.keyNote: The left and right arrow keys also switch, and the highlight slides in the same way.

reshuffle.name: Cards reshuffling on filter
reshuffle.tagline: GSAP Flip · the difference, replayed in the layout phase
reshuffle.summary: When the software page's record shelf is filtered by category, the sleeves that stay slide from their old cells to their new positions and the others fade out. Nine coloured tiles stand in for the sleeves here.
reshuffle.note: Every tile stays in the DOM and the filter only toggles display. The timing is what matters: the state has to be captured in the click handler, before React re-renders, and Flip.from runs in a layout-phase useGSAP, so the new positions are never painted first. Entering tiles fade in from scale 0.94 and leaving tiles do the opposite, 30ms apart. The filter buttons here are ordinary buttons; the sliding highlight is in the filter tabs study. The shelf on a phone works the same way, three sleeves per row.
reshuffle.gridNote: Rapid clicks do not break it: each click first finishes the previous reshuffle if it is still running and clears the styles it wrote, then starts the new one.
reshuffle.label: Grid · filter and reshuffle
reshuffle.lede: Press Round, Square or Line: the three tiles that stay slide into the first row and the other six fade out. Press All and they return the way they came. If it is too fast, choose the slow motion; to see it without the effect, turn the animation off.
reshuffle.readoutIdle: All nine are here and nothing is filtered yet. Press any shape above.
reshuffle.readout: That change: {stay} stayed, sliding to wherever their place now is; {enter} faded in, {leave} faded out.
reshuffle.readoutNone: That change had no animation: {stay} stayed, {enter} appeared and {leave} disappeared, all at the same moment, so you cannot tell which tile went where. The animation is there to solve that.

statue.name: A 3D statue built in code
statue.summary: The bronze Kobe statue from the idols page. It is built in code from twelve capsules plus a few spheres and boxes, with no model file, and it is rendered only while it turns; once it stops, no new frames are drawn. A wireframe view and a frame counter are added here to show both.
statue.note: The statue uses a single metal material and a base. The limbs are capsules from one joint to the next, oriented by rotating from the y axis with setFromUnitVectors. The jersey number is painted once on a canvas and applied as a texture, with no font file and no glyph mesh. The canvas renders on demand: a turn writes the angle to a ref and calls invalidate() for one frame, and nothing is rendered after it stops. A mouse turns it by dragging; touch screens and keyboards use the two arrow buttons, because capturing swipes on a phone would conflict with page scrolling. Without WebGL, or under Save-Data, a photograph is shown here.
statue.label: Statue · capsules · render on demand
statue.lede: Drag the statue, or press the arrows at the lower right, and watch the frame count below: the number increases only while the statue turns and stays the same once it stops. Then switch to the wireframe to see the basic shapes it is made of.
statue.frameNote: A typical 3D scene redraws 60 frames a second whether or not anything changes. This one stops rendering once it stops turning, so leaving the page open uses no extra power.

changelog.name: A year rail that follows the scroll
changelog.summary: A personal history written in the format of software version numbers. The year column on the left shows one row at a time and switches to the matching year when an entry crosses the middle of the viewport.
changelog.lede: Scroll down: as each entry crosses the middle of the viewport, the year on the left switches to that entry's year. Rest the pointer on a dot, or focus it with Tab, to see the exact date of that entry.
changelog.title: Changelog
changelog.listAria: Personal milestones, numbered like software releases
changelog.note: The rows are read from the database and edited in the admin. This list used to be on the About page; since October the career section there lists three cities with this same component and year column, and the version list is kept only here. The year column is a stack of years behind a window one row tall. As each entry crosses the middle of the viewport, ScrollTrigger snaps the stack to that entry's year, so the reader can see which year the current entry belongs to. Each node shows its exact date on hover or focus: it appears on back.out and disappears on the reversed ease at 2.2× speed.

screening.name: A stills wall with a full-screen viewer
screening.summary: The stills wall from the film pages: stills are laid out in six columns, and a click opens a full-screen viewer. It is a native dialog, the still is as large as the viewport allows, and the arrow keys, the buttons or a swipe change the still.
screening.lede: Press any still to open the full-screen viewer. Use the arrow keys, the buttons on either side or a swipe to change the still; press Escape, the backdrop or the close button to leave.
screening.note: Each still is a link to its image file, so without JavaScript a click opens that image directly. With JavaScript, the click opens the full-screen viewer instead: dialog.showModal() takes focus and makes the background unclickable, page scrolling uses the site's shared lock (Lenis stop + overflow hidden, then scrollTo → start → refresh on close), and after closing, focus returns to the still that opened it. Opening is a 0.35s fade with the picture scaling from 0.96 to 1; changing the still slides the next one in by 24px from the direction of travel; closing fades out on power2.in and then calls close(). State is cleaned up only in the native close event, so Escape, the backdrop and the button all run the same code. The stills and captions here are from the page for 大话西游, including the rights line.

lights.name: Light and dark theme switch
lights.summary: The site's theme switch, the one in the footer. It changes the theme state in three places inside a view transition; the sound, the vibration and the fade start on the same frame.
lights.note: The switch changes three things: the 'fhfs-theme' entry in localStorage, the data-theme attribute and the 'fhfs:theme' event, and multiple instances of the switch stay in sync through that event. The change is wrapped in document.startViewTransition, which globals.css sets to a 1.2s cross-fade: the whole page fades between an old and a new snapshot, and elements are not recoloured one by one. On the same frame there is a synthesised square-wave click (one AudioContext, created on the first click, with no audio file) and a 10ms vibration; this is the only place on the site that uses sound and vibration together. The server does not know the theme, so it renders the light theme first and reads the real value in a layout effect; in a passive effect, readers in dark mode would see one frame of the switch in the wrong state.
lights.label: Lights
lights.body: The site's theme switch, the one in the footer, shown here at two and a half times its size. The sound, the vibration and the 1.2s cross-fade start on the same frame.

readingChip.name: Reading progress bar
readingChip.summary: The capsule at the bottom left of a post page: a thin progress bar and a percentage. It normally appears only on post pages; here it shows this page's progress.
readingChip.note: Scroll events are throttled with rAF, and each update writes only a transform and a textContent, with no layout change and no React re-render. The entrance is a single 0.35s float-in; after that the capsule does not move, and only the fill's scaleX changes with the scroll. It has role=progressbar and aria-valuenow, so a screen reader can report the progress. In the layout it appears only on post routes, /blog/…; the pattern is anchored at both ends, otherwise the tag listing pages would match as well. This page is made long on purpose, so there is something to scroll.
readingChip.label: Reading progress
readingChip.body: The capsule at the bottom left. It normally appears only on post pages; here it shows this page's progress.

radialFan.name: Radial pop-out menu
radialFan.summary: The plus button at the bottom right of a post page on a phone: four buttons pop out along a 90° arc, and closing plays the same timeline in reverse. It does not exist on wide screens.
radialFan.note: The four buttons are placed along the quarter circle from 180° to 270° at radius 104, on elastic.out(1, 0.5) with a 0.05s stagger, and the plus rotates 135° into a cross. The timeline is created once and switched with play() / reverse(), so a tap partway through reverses it directly and nothing queues. Closing uses easeReverse at 2.2× speed. It appears on phones only, because on wide screens the top navigation already provides the same functions.
radialFan.label: Radial fan
radialFan.body: The plus at the bottom right: tap it and four buttons pop out along a 90° arc; tap again and it plays in reverse. On the site it appears only on phones; here it is shown on wide screens too.

overture.name: The opening animation on first visit
overture.tagline: Once per session · a sessionStorage key
overture.summary: A 0.9s animation on the first page of each session: a black screen, a lamp cord coming down, then a glow that lights the page. It plays once per session; the button here clears the record and reloads so you can see it again.
overture.note: The animation is played by OvertureLight in the layout, and whether it has played is stored in sessionStorage. It plays only on arrival and cannot be mounted separately on this page, so the button calls forgetOverture() to clear the record and then reloads this page, and the layout plays it again on load. It also triggers the home headline's line-by-line rise.
overture.label: Opening animation
overture.body: A 0.9s animation on the first page of each session: a black screen, a lamp cord coming down, then a glow that lights the page.
overture.reducedNote: Your system has reduced motion turned on, so the opening animation is skipped and a reload will not show it. Turn that setting off and try again.

door.name: The entrance transition through the sign
door.tagline: Opening the home page directly · through the ring
door.summary: When the home page is opened directly, the brick wall and the neon sign are shown first. The entrance transition goes through the ring: the letters go dark, the ring stays, the paper colour appears inside the ring and grows to fill the screen.
door.note: Whether the sign is shown is decided by the inline script in lib/client/splash when the home page is opened directly, before the first paint (it sets data-splash on the html element), once per session; navigation within the site never shows it. So the button in this study calls forgetSplash() to clear the record in sessionStorage and then does a full page load of the home page. How the sign is drawn and lit is covered in study 08; this one only shows the entrance transition.
door.label: Entrance transition
door.body: The brick wall and neon sign shown when the home page is opened directly. The entrance transition goes through the ring.
door.action: Go to the home page and replay

veil.name: The frosted page transition
veil.summary: On any in-site link, a frosted layer covers the current page first and is removed once the new page has loaded. It runs on every page change, so a button here plays it in place.
veil.note: RouteTransition intercepts clicks on in-site links: it covers the page with the frosted layer, waits for the new route's content to load and then removes the layer, so the page changes while covered and the reader never sees a blank screen. External links, file links marked data-no-transition and clicks with a modifier key are not intercepted. It only appears during a page change, and a link to the current page does not trigger it, so RouteTransition has one event used only by the lab: the button covers the page in place, holds briefly and uncovers it, using the same cover and reveal, without changing the page or the scroll position.
veil.label: Page transition
veil.body: On any in-site link, a frosted layer covers the current page first and is removed once the new page has loaded. Here it plays in place, without changing the page.

island.name: The top navigation island
island.summary: The capsule navigation at the top of every page. On a wide screen it folds after 48px of scrolling down and unfolds after 48px of scrolling back up. Scroll down to see it.
island.note: The navigation is at the top of every page, including this one, so nothing extra is mounted here: scroll down and it folds, scroll back and it unfolds. Folding depends on the direction and distance of the scroll and not on the position in the page: 48px down folds it and 48px up unfolds it anywhere on the page, so the navigation can be brought back at any time. At widths of 1024px and above it starts open with six entries and folds into a capsule on scroll; the highlight on its rim is the filter from study 15. This page is made long on purpose, so there is something to scroll.
island.label: The island
island.body: At the top of the page. On a wide screen it folds after 48px of scrolling down and unfolds after 48px of scrolling back up.

kobe.statueTitle: The statue pointing at the sky
kobe.statueBody: January 22, 2006, against the Raptors: 81 points. At the buzzer he pointed his right hand at the sky. On February 8, 2024 the Lakers raised a 19-foot bronze outside Crypto.com Arena in that pose, wearing the number 8 jersey, with the game's box score on the base. The one here is built in code after the same pose.
